title: What They Remembered
subtitle: Past-Life Sessions, Honestly Told
description_paragraphs: She described the staircase before I asked about the house. She counted forty-one steps, and then she said "forty-one, always forty-one" in a voice that was not the voice she had been using with me.

That is the kind of moment this book is full of, and it is also the kind of moment that usually gets written up as something it is not. A regression session is testimony: an accurate record of what a person said and felt in a chair, and not a record of the world outside it. Almost every book on this shelf slides from the first to the second somewhere around the verbs, and readers who go and check one claim tend not to come back.

What They Remembered reports eight sessions end to end — the words, the silences, the crying, the four minutes a man could not speak. Where a session touched something that could be looked up, it was looked up, and the book says plainly what came back. Four times out of eight, what came back was nothing, and the book says nothing in that word. One session did produce a match, and the chapter that reports it spends three pages explaining why the match is worth less than it looks.
It is not a debunking. It takes the chair seriously and it takes you seriously enough not to dress a session up as proof.

One woman counted forty-one stairs and stopped waking at three in the morning. A man who had not stood on a beach in twenty years described a wet rope and could not speak for two minutes, and booked a swimming lesson eleven weeks later. A woman produced a name she could not pronounce, and six hours of searching found nothing — which the book reports as nothing, because that is what it was. Another session went nowhere at all: an hour of a man lying quietly, reporting the colour behind his eyelids. It is in here too, because a book with eight sessions in it and no empty ones would be telling you something false about what booking one actually buys.

Along the way: what the hour before a session decides, and why it matters more than the induction. The six words that smuggle a claim, and the plainer ones that do not. The question a practitioner should never ask, and the sessions that taught that lesson the hard way. What the documentary record can and cannot settle, and the arithmetic that quietly dissolves most apparent matches. And the ordinary explanations — forgotten sources, suggestion, the mind's talent for narrative — laid out at full strength rather than waved at, because a reader who has not met them cannot judge anything else in here.

author_bio: Thea Bramwell is a pen name. The sessions in this book are written accounts rather than transcripts, built from the shape that regression sessions take — and the book says so on its first page, at length, rather than in small type at the back. It was written for readers who are drawn to this work and who have stopped trusting the shelf it sits on.
back_cover:
She described the staircase before I asked about the house.

This book reports eight sessions in full: the words, the pauses, the crying, the things that came out in a voice the person does not use. Where a session touched something that can be looked up — a name, a date, a place, an object — it was looked up, and the book tells you what came back, including the times it came back empty.

What it will not do is dress a session up as proof. A regression is testimony, not history, and the difference is the whole book. You will finish it knowing what happens minute by minute in a session, what a practitioner should refuse to promise you, how to prepare for your own, and how to read every other account on this shelf without either swallowing it whole or throwing it out.
